keyTakeaways: Define whether the production needs language translation, audio access, an audience delivery method, or several of these together.
English surtitles translate a live non-English performance; accessibility captions may also identify speakers, music, effects, and off-stage sound.
Projection and mobile viewing are delivery choices, not definitions of what the text contains.
Public listings can say “English subtitles,” while the internal specification should name content, languages, operator, testing, and fallback.

faq.question: When does a Fringe show need English surtitles?
faq.answer: Use prepared English surtitles when audiences need reviewed translation for a live performance spoken or sung in another language.

faq.question: When does a Fringe show need accessibility captions?
faq.answer: Captions may be needed when D/deaf or hard-of-hearing audiences require dialogue plus relevant speaker, music, sound-effect, or off-stage information.

faq.question: Are projection and mobile viewing different kinds of text?
faq.answer: No. They are delivery methods. The production must first decide whether the content is translation, accessibility captioning, or both.

faq.question: Is mobile viewing automatically the most accessible option?
faq.answer: No. Device access, screen size, venue policy, connectivity, audience preference, front-of-house guidance, and a fallback all matter.

glossary.definition: Prepared translation displayed in time with a live performance spoken or sung in another language.
Audience text that may represent speech, speakers, music, sound effects, and off-stage sound.
The route by which audiences receive text, such as shared projection, a mobile viewer, or both.
The internal definition of text content, languages, display route, operator, review, testing, and fallback.
The operator's work of triggering and recovering prepared text in time with the performance.
